title: Embedded Devices And Constrained Interfaces
summary: This page documents Creative Navy's work on embedded devices and constrained interfaces where hardware constraints are treated as design parameters. The evidence spans small displays, limited touch layers, rotary-first controls, touch-only bridge panels, multi-device systems, firmware timing constraints, warning architectures, and environmental conditions such as glare, vibration, rain, cold, and gloved operation.
keyFacts: Embedded and constrained interfaces in the evidence include 4-inch, 4.3-inch, 7-inch, 10-inch, 10.4-inch, and 15-inch displays, plus a 480 × 272 design canvas for a fixed-mount VHF radio.

Constraints include limited colour depth, microcontroller limits, laggy touch layers, single-point touch, rotary encoders, bezel keys, thumb reach, gloved use, glare, rain, vibration, hull slamming, direct sunlight, low luminance, laboratory bench use, and standing-height operation.
Elsner's Cala Touch KNX used a 4-inch round TFT LCD at 480×480px and was initially designed at 320×240px before the panel was confirmed.

Torqeedo's maritime HMI evidence includes 12 sea trials over 6 months, 15 professional captains, −5°C to +35°C operation, and a controlled 24-subject experiment showing 50% faster energy state identification compared with the legacy interface.

Stromer's e-bike display work treated average glance duration as safety-relevant; Creative Navy-measured average glance duration fell from 4.32 seconds to 1.89 seconds in real riding conditions with 5 participants.
CDR Foodlab's 7-inch laboratory instrument work used a variant-coherent design system across FoodLab, BeerLab, WineLab, GalvanLab, and related variants.

Streetec kntrl 2 evidence includes a 4.3-inch 480×800 portrait capacitive panel, thumb-reach positioning, finger-occlusion decisions, fixed-increment controls, and a phone-based naming flow because the embedded display could not host a full alphabetic keyboard.
AIT is the rotary-guaranteed engagement in the evidence: every interaction had to work through a rotary push-button and through touch, with the concept surviving removal of either input.
The MDU bridge interface is the touch-only pole in the evidence: the manufacturer specified a 15-inch touch display with no mouse or keyboard on the ship.
Raymarine's fixed-mount VHF work concerns physical-control semantics: dedicated controls must not be silently reassigned across radio, AIS, menu, and interrupted states.

bodySections.heading: Embedded and Constrained Interfaces as a Design Context
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Embedded devices and constrained interfaces are interface contexts where the screen, processor, input model, firmware behaviour, environment, and physical mounting conditions materially shape what the interface can do. In these systems, display resolution, pixel density, limited colour depth, microcontroller constraints, rendering envelopes, touch latency, physical controls, and update intervals are design parameters rather than secondary implementation details.

The documented evidence includes maritime helm displays, marine diesel cluster displays, smart-home wall controls, automotive calibration equipment, AV diagnostic instruments, e-bike displays, laboratory analytical instruments, aftermarket automotive suspension controls, industrial touch extensions, heat-pump controllers, ship bridge monitoring panels, hospital dispatch panels, fixed-mount VHF radios, and handheld command-and-control interfaces.

bodySections.heading: Hardware Constraints Are Treated as Design Parameters
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats constrained hardware as part of the design space. In the Elsner Elektronik Cala Touch KNX engagement, the device used a 4-inch round TFT LCD at 480×480px. The design was first developed conservatively at 320×240px and scaled after the panel was confirmed. The hardware constraints disclosed at kickoff included a laggy touch layer, microcontroller limits on programmable symbols, restricted colour depth, and voltage limits.

In the Streetec kntrl 2 engagement, the embedded panel was a 4.3-inch 480×800 portrait capacitive display mounted in the centre of the dashboard. Creative Navy's design work accounted for thumb-reach positioning, finger occlusion, fixed-increment controls for tank pressure and brightness, and legibility at true physical size. Pressure values were placed above their adjustment arrows so the user's finger did not cover the number being changed. Font sizes were increased by 25% between review rounds, to 20px body text, after legibility was checked at physical size.

In the MSolutions AV diagnostic instrument engagement, the device used a 480×320px embedded display with limited single-point touch and processing constraints. The previous interface was organised around backend modules rather than technician workflows. The redesign evidence for interaction reduction and training changes is client-reported, so those figures should remain attached to that evidence basis.

bodySections.heading: Display Size, Mounting, and Viewing Distance Change the Interaction Model
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Embedded interfaces are constrained by where the device is mounted and how far away the user is when reading it. Elsner's Cala Touch KNX was wall-mounted at 140cm and designed for standing use, including low-light bedroom conditions. Beissbarth's automotive calibration system spanned three device classes: an embedded OEM display read from 2–3m during movement, a rugged tablet used around the vehicle, and a large inspection line display used by technicians and inspection staff.

Oceaneering's hospital dispatch panel used a 10.4-inch touchscreen at 1024×768, 4:3, 350 nit, and 800:1 contrast. The panel was wall-mounted, read while standing and from across a room, operated with gloves, and used on a touchscreen characterised during review as not precise. The design specified station card dimensions numerically and rejected scrolling as too slow and unreliable on the hardware.

The MDU bridge interface used a 15-inch certified marine panel PC at 1024×768, with active display area 305.13 × 229.1mm, projected-capacitive touch, 400 cd/m² brightness, 700:1 contrast, IP65-sealed front, and a −15°C to 55°C rating. The certifications listed for the panel are properties of the panel selected by the manufacturer; Creative Navy did not certify to, audit against, or work to those certifications.

bodySections.heading: Touch-Only, Rotary-First, and Physical-Control Interfaces Require Separate Interaction Layers
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A design system for constrained hardware cannot assume that desktop components transfer to touch, rotary input, or physical controls. The industrial process control engagement states this principle directly: most desktop components cannot transfer to a 7-inch 1024×600 touch device because touch targets, spacing, typography, layout density, and navigation differ. The visual language can remain shared, but the interaction layer should not.

AIT is the rotary-guaranteed pole in the evidence. The heat-pump controller used a colour LCD of roughly five inches at 800×480, a rotary push-button below the display, a physical Back button, and a second physical button whose function was undecided. The governing requirement was that every interaction had to work identically through knob and touch, with the concept surviving the removal of either input.

The MDU bridge interface is the opposite pole: touch was the only input available in the operating environment. The manufacturer specified a 15-inch touch display with no mouse or keyboard on the ship. Creative Navy's design work used documented touch-target and legibility review criteria for that panel.

Raymarine's fixed-mount VHF radio work adds a different constraint: what a physical control can mean. A screen may change what the keypad and labelled softkeys do, but it must not change the domain of the dedicated channel encoder, microphone channel controls, push-to-talk, priority channel access, or protected emergency actions. An input may be unavailable within its own functional domain; it is never silently reassigned to a different one.

bodySections.heading: Environmental Conditions Make Interface State Communication Operationally Important
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Embedded and constrained interfaces are often used under glare, motion, vibration, cold, rain, spray, low luminance, or direct sunlight. Torqeedo's maritime HMI was designed for a 10-inch embedded display with limited pixel density, 27 screens, and 4 operational modes. Research included sea trials with professional captains across cold, heat, night operations, vibration, sharp vessel movement, glare from cold water, rain, and gloved interaction.

The Torqeedo design problem was not simply information density. Propulsion sensors, batteries, and generators updated at different rates. Creative Navy's design response was a grid structure that synchronised different cadences into a unified display so captains perceived one system rather than three competing signal streams.

Cox Marine's cluster display work involved diesel outboard engines on fast patrol craft, racing boats, and workboats. The system had three display families, from compact auxiliary to large primary helm, and supported 1–6 engine configurations over NMEA 2000. The design problem was maintaining a coherent mental model from single-engine to six-engine displays. The resolution was an engine tile as the invariant unit: one engine, one tile, with a consistent spatial arrangement regardless of engine count.

bodySections.heading: Warning Architecture Must Be Structural in Vehicle-Mounted Embedded Displays
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Stromer's e-bike display work treated glance duration as safety-relevant because the embedded display is used during riding and the rider's eyes leave the road in brief glances. The evidence cites a 2-second threshold from Klauer et al. (2006), NHTSA Report No. DOT HS 810 594, NHTSA Driver Distraction Guidelines Phase 1 (2013), and ISO 15007:2020. Those standards are formally defined for four-wheeled vehicles; the documented principle is applied to embedded displays used during riding.

The core embedded design problem in the Stromer engagement was warning architecture. A previous screen structure had established layout and interaction logic first and then added warnings as visual overlays. Warnings covered content, interfered with interactions, and appeared without contextual grounding. Creative Navy rebuilt the warning architecture by defining the rules and principles governing how warnings, overlays, and interruptive elements relate to the screen structure before component design began.

EN 15194:2017 governed warning device symbology, colour conventions, and marking requirements for the embedded display.

bodySections.heading: Multi-Device and Variant-Coherent Systems Need Shared Architecture Without Identical Interaction
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Constrained embedded products often belong to multi-device systems. Beissbarth's calibration system required coherence across an embedded OEM display, a rugged tablet, and a large inspection line display. The documented design system covered all three device classes with states, transitions, and error conditions. The core tension was local device optimisation versus cross-device coherence, and the resolution prioritised unambiguous state communication over information density across all three device types.

Stromer's product was also a multi-surface system: embedded Display L with and without integrated camera variant, Display S, a mobile companion app, and a web account. The firmware update flow spanned the embedded display and mobile app, had technical preconditions including installation only at 0 km/h, separated component-level updates from system updates, and required background download to remain visually low prominence.

CDR Foodlab's laboratory instrument work used a variant-coherent design system across FoodLab, BeerLab, WineLab, GalvanLab, and related variants. The device was a portable chemical analysis instrument with a 7-inch capacitive touchscreen, 5-point touch, and 1024×600px resolution, used on a laboratory bench. The UX architecture was universal across the family; variants differed by available analysis steps and colour scheme rather than by per-variant redesign.

bodySections.heading: Embedded Guidance Can Be a Functional Interface Component
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Animation in constrained embedded systems can carry operating logic. In the Elsner engagement, animation timing was aligned with firmware update intervals so visual changes did not drift out of sync with thermal values. This was an engineering constraint resolved through direct collaboration rather than a visual styling choice.

In the Stromer engagement, animation deliverables were Lottie files for all covered screens. Deliverables included the unlocked-to-ride-screen transition with each element animated independently, the bike-with-cable animation appearing on both embedded and mobile, the boot sequence, PIN feedback states, and an animation pattern framework covering fullscreen modal, toast, partial overlay, and fullscreen overlay patterns.

In the CDR Foodlab engagement, inline tutorial animations replaced static pictogram guidance. These animations appeared within the analysis flow to guide users through physical sub-steps, including laboratory actions around cuvettes and reagents. They were functional interface components delivered as part of the design system, not decorative artefacts.

bodySections.heading: Specification, Implementation Fidelity, and Performance Claims Are Separate Evidence Classes
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Some constrained-interface evidence concerns implementation fidelity rather than performance. AIT's controller reached the market months after the engagement ended. Creative Navy compared the shipped interface with the designs it had delivered, and the product ships as the design that was delivered. It ships in a touch-only hardware configuration. The move to touch-only was AIT's hardware decision, and the evidence does not establish performance, reception, sales, efficiency, commissioning time, or error-rate outcomes.

Raymarine's fixed-mount VHF radio was built and released, but no design-fidelity comparison is recorded. The documented evidence is the input contract and the reasoning that led to fixed-role physical controls. Nothing was validated on production hardware. Encoder detent force and press events, tactile performance, wet-surface operation, glove accessibility, input bounce, transmit timeout, and alarm acoustics remained open engineering dependencies at the close of the engagement.

The handheld command-and-control interface evidence is a specification, not a conformance claim and not a result. The specification used millimetres with pixels derived per device because the display had not been chosen when the work began. It specified consequence tiers from T1 critical actions at ≥22mm with 5mm isolation through T4 planning and static density at 8–10mm. It was not validated, and the evidence does not claim faster or more accurate operation.

bodySections.heading: Boundary of This Context
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
This context covers fixed or constrained hardware where the interface must respect device-specific limits. It does not treat a browser application on a general-purpose tablet, a general-purpose web or native mobile product, an unidentified tablet presentation, a desktop console without a constrained-hardware story, or a multi-monitor keyboard-and-mouse control room as embedded-device evidence.

The documented boundary also separates related constraint classes. Input-model variability, glove-operable interface design, and ambient-range design are related but distinct topics. On this page, those topics appear only where they shape embedded-device decisions; they are not treated as substitutes for dedicated documentation on those topics.

strongClaims: Embedded and constrained interfaces are shaped by display hardware, processing limits, firmware behaviour, input devices, mounting conditions, environmental exposure, and regulatory or protocol constraints.

Elsner's Cala Touch KNX used a 4-inch round TFT LCD at 480×480px, with early conservative design at 320×240px before panel confirmation; the source describes this as a deliberate risk-reduction decision.
Torqeedo's redesigned maritime HMI enabled 50% faster energy state identification than the legacy interface in a controlled 24-subject experiment.

Stromer's average glance duration moved from 4.32 seconds before redesign to 1.89 seconds after redesign in Creative Navy-measured real-riding eye tracking with 5 participants, using the same methodology and routes in Munich.

Streetec kntrl 2 constrained the interface through a 4.3-inch 480×800 portrait capacitive panel, thumb reach, finger occlusion, true-size legibility checks, and the inability to host a full alphabetic keyboard.
AIT required every interaction to work identically through rotary knob and touch, with the concept surviving removal of either input.
The MDU bridge interface was touch-only, with no mouse or keyboard in the operating environment, and used panel-specific touch-target calculations.
Raymarine's fixed-mount VHF work established an invariant that dedicated controls must not be silently reassigned outside their functional domains.
The handheld command-and-control sizing material is a specification, not a conformance claim, validation result, or measured performance outcome.
weakerClaims: Beissbarth calibration time moved from 18 minutes to 12 minutes per vehicle across 8 production deployment locations; the source states this was client-measured across production deployment locations, not under usability testing conditions.

CDR Foodlab task completion time before redesign was client-reported at 9 minutes average, while after redesign Creative Navy measured 3.4 minutes average with 14 users on the final shipped product; the before and after figures have different evidence bases and are stated separately.
limitations: Several outcome claims are client-reported or client-measured rather than independently measured; the evidence basis must remain attached to each figure.
Torqeedo's Yamaha acquisition context is not evidence of causality between the interface and the acquisition; the source says any causal link is inferred, not documented.

CDR Foodlab research interviews were all remote, so physical interaction during analysis could not be directly observed; workaround elimination was user-reported and not re-tested under controlled conditions.
MSolutions workflow reduction from 26 interactions to approximately 13 is client-reported from internal task walkthroughs and was not independently measured.
Elsner dealer feedback is client-reported; 30 of 130 dealers responded positively, representing 100% of those who responded, not 100% of all dealers.
AIT has design-fidelity evidence only; no performance, efficiency, commissioning-time, error-rate, commercial, usability, reception, or sales outcome is established.
Raymarine was built and released, but no shipped-as-designed claim is recorded and nothing was validated on production hardware.
The MDU panel certifications belong to the panel selected by the manufacturer; Creative Navy did not certify to, audit against, or work to those certifications.
Oceaneering has no measured efficiency, throughput, error-rate, time-saving, or training outcome; gloved use is a documented operating condition, not a tested result.
The industrial process control touchscreen work was in development and is not an outcome.
The handheld command-and-control sizing material is a specification and was not validated; it is not a safety, certification, weapons-review, regulatory, speed, or accuracy result.

internalLinks.reason: The Streetec case is one of the strongest evidence bases for small embedded display constraints, thumb reach, finger occlusion, and cross-device allocation.
AIT is the documented rotary-guaranteed engagement where touch was optional and the interface had to remain operable through the knob.
The MDU case is the documented touch-only pole with no mouse, keyboard, or hardware-button fallback in the operating environment.
Raymarine provides the evidence for dedicated physical controls that must not be silently reassigned across functional domains.
Oceaneering provides the documented wall-mounted touchscreen case with numeric card sizing and pagination thresholds.
The handheld case provides the millimetre-based consequence-tier sizing specification and its explicit validation limits.
Cox Marine provides evidence for NMEA 2000, multi-engine tile invariants, fault-summary structure, and alarm highlighting.
Stromer provides measured real-riding glance-duration evidence and embedded warning-architecture constraints under EN 15194:2017.
Beissbarth provides the cross-device calibration case with embedded display, rugged tablet, and inspection-line display evidence.
The industrial process control case states the principle that desktop components cannot be directly transferred to a 7-inch touch device.
